The Romans conquered the Greeks but respected their culture enough to allow them to teach their children. Many Latin letters corresponded closely enough to Greek letters to allow many Greek words to be Latinized without much difficulty, but the letter upsilon, meaning simple Y, although similar to i, was different enough that folks figured it deserved its own place in the Latin alphabet, but it was difficult for Romans to pronounce correctly and they didn't actually consider it a Latin letter even though it was amongst the other letters. Unlike the other letters which were each named after the sound they make, Y was instead called i graeca or ypsilon. In Greek the upper case of the letter looks like Y, but the lowercase looks like a stylized u, which is why in English the letter is called upsilon. The correct pronunciation of the letter in ancient Greek and ancient Latin is generally difficult for English speakers but it's generally easy for German speakers because German has a letter that is either the same or very similar. I can't recall offhand whether modern Greek has retained the letter's pronunciation. Often Romans would simply pronounce it the same as their letter i which is like an English hard e, such as in the word feet.
